# line_wrap - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/line-wrap/

## Expand description

Efficiently insert line endings.

If you have a buffer full of data and want to insert any sort of regularly-spaced separator,
this will do it with a minimum of data copying. Commonly, this is to insert `\n` (see `lf()`) or `\r\n` (`crlf()`), but
any byte sequence can be used.

- Pick a line ending. For single byte separators, see `ByteLineEnding`, or for two bytes,`TwoByteLineEnding`. For arbitrary byte slices, use`SliceLineEnding`.
- Call `line_wrap`.
- Your data has been rearranged in place with the specified line ending inserted.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use line_wrap::*;
// suppose we have 80 bytes of data in a buffer and we want to wrap as per MIME.
// Buffer is large enough to hold line endings.
let mut data = vec![0; 82];
assert_eq!(2, line_wrap(&mut data, 80, 76, &crlf()));
// first line of zeroes
let mut expected_data = vec![0; 76];
// line ending
expected_data.extend_from_slice(b"\r\n");
// next line
expected_data.extend_from_slice(&[0, 0, 0, 0]);
assert_eq!(expected_data, data);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#performance)Performance

On an i7 6850k:

- 10 byte input, 1 byte line length takes ~60ns (~160MiB/s)
- 100 byte input, 10 byte lines takes ~60ns (~1.6GiB/s)
- Startup costs dominate at these small lengths

- 1,000 byte input, 100 byte lines takes ~65ns (~15GiB/s)
- 10,000 byte input, 100 byte lines takes ~550ns (~17GiB/s)
- In general, `SliceLineEncoding`is about 75% the speed of the fixed-length impls.

Naturally, try `cargo +nightly bench` on your hardware to get more representative data.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Byte](https://docs.rs/struct.ByteLineEnding.html)- Line - Ending
- A single byte line ending.
- [Slice](https://docs.rs/struct.SliceLineEnding.html)- Line - Ending
- A byte slice line ending.
- [TwoByte](https://docs.rs/struct.TwoByteLineEnding.html)- Line - Ending
- A double byte line ending.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Line](https://docs.rs/trait.LineEnding.html)- Ending
- Writes line endings.

# rand - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand/^0.8.5/

## Expand description

Utilities for random number generation

Rand provides utilities to generate random numbers, to convert them to useful types and distributions, and some randomness-related algorithms.

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick Start

To get you started quickly, the easiest and highest-level way to get
a random value is to use [ random()](https://docs.rs/fn.random.html); alternatively you can use

[. The](https://docs.rs/fn.thread_rng.html)

`thread_rng()`[trait provides a useful API on all RNGs, while the](https://docs.rs/trait.Rng.html)

`Rng`[and](https://docs.rs/distributions/index.html)

`distributions`[modules provide further functionality on top of RNGs.](https://docs.rs/seq/index.html)

`seq````
use rand::prelude::*;
if rand::random() { // generates a boolean
    // Try printing a random unicode code point (probably a bad idea)!
    println!("char: {}", rand::random::<char>());
}
let mut rng = rand::thread_rng();
let y: f64 = rng.gen(); // generates a float between 0 and 1
let mut nums: Vec<i32> = (1..100).collect();
nums.shuffle(&mut rng);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#the-book)The Book

For the user guide and further documentation, please read
[The Rust Rand Book](https://rust-random.github.io/book).

- Retrieve the lazily-initialized thread-local random number generator,
seeded by the system. Intended to be used in method chaining style,
e.g. `thread_rng().gen::<i32>()`, or cached locally, e.g.`let mut rng = thread_rng();`. Invoked by the`Default`trait, making`ThreadRng::default()`equivalent.

# About Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/about

Docs.rs is an
            [open source](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs)
            documentation host for crates of the
            [Rust Programming Language](https://www.rust-lang.org/).
            All libraries published to [crates.io](https://crates.io)
            are documented. If you just published a crate, your crate is likely
            still in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

            The source code of Docs.rs is available on
            [GitHub](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs). If
            you ever encounter an issue, don't hesitate to report it! (And
            thanks in advance!)

Currently running Docs.rs version is: **0.0.0 (964c90a45859fd8f9076e3cbe58470a5a4f4d4f7 2026-07-01 )**

Summaries of the documentation build processes [are available at /releases/](https://docs.rs/releases).

            JavaScript in support of documentation is allowed but not guaranteed to work on docs.rs. What that
            means: If you write documentation that inlines some JavaScript (like
            [KaTeX](https://katex.org/)), that's allowed, and
            will probably work today but may break in the future.

However, it's not allowed to put JavaScript or other content in docs published on docs.rs for the purpose of tracking visitors. For instance, adding Google Analytics scripts, tracking pixels, or site verification for services like Google Search Console. Crates that do this will have the relevant versions removed and may be blocked from docs.rs.

            Docs.rs is run and maintained by the [Docs.rs team](https://www.rust-lang.org/governance/teams/dev-tools#team-docs-rs).
            You can find us in #t-docs-rs on [Zulip](https://rust-lang.zulipchat.com/#narrow/stream/356853-t-docs-rs).

# Builds

Source: https://docs.rs/about/builds

Docs.rs automatically builds documentation for crates released on [crates.io](https://crates.io/).
                It may take a while to build your crate, depending on how many crates are in [the queue](https://docs.rs/releases/queue).

                All crates are built in a sandbox using the nightly release of the Rust compiler.
                The current version in use is `rustc 1.98.0-nightly (c397dae80 2026-07-02)`.

                The README displayed on docs.rs follows Cargo’s `package.readme` rules.
                If `readme` is not set, docs.rs will look for `README.md`, `README.txt`, or `README` in the crate root.
                Set `readme = "path/to/file"` to use a custom file, `readme = true` to use `README.md`, or `readme = false` to disable the README.

                To recognize Docs.rs from your Rust code, you can test for the `docsrs` cfg, e.g.:

```
```
                To recognize Docs.rs from `build.rs` files, you can test for the environment variable `DOCS_RS`, e.g.:

`if var.is_ok `
              All targets other than `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` are cross-compiled. For implementation reasons, this is unlikely to change for the foreseeable future.

                You can configure how your crate is built by adding [package metadata](https://docs.rs/metadata) to your `Cargo.toml`, e.g.:

```
[]
 = ["--cfg", "my_cfg"]
```
`#[cfg(my_cfg)]` (not to be confused with `#[cfg(doc)]`) can be used for conditional compilation.
                This approach is also useful for setting
                When you start using docs.rs metadata or `#[cfg(docsrs)]` in your code, you might run into issues
                where your code builds fine locally but fails on docs.rs.
                To avoid this, you can add [ cargo docs-rs](https://github.com/dtolnay/cargo-docs-rs) to
                your test-suite.
                While it doesn't perfectly replicate our build environment, it can catch many common issues.

                The Docs.rs [README](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/blob/master/README.md#build-subcommand) describes how to build
                unpublished crate documentation locally using the same build environment as the Docs.rs build agent.

                Missing dependencies are a common reason for failed builds.
                Docs.rs dependencies are managed through
                [crates-build-env](https://github.com/rust-lang/crates-build-env).
                See [Forge](https://forge.rust-lang.org/docs-rs/add-dependencies.html) for how to add a dependency.

                Most of the sandbox is a read-only file system, including the source directory of your crate and its dependencies.
                If your `build.rs` generates files that are relevant for documentation, consider writing to the
                [cargo output directory](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/environment-variables.html#environment-variables-cargo-sets-for-crates),
                passed in the environment variable `OUT_DIR`.

All the builds are executed inside a sandbox with limited resources. The current limits are:

| Available RAM | 6.44 GB |
| Maximum rustdoc execution time | 15m |
| Maximum size of a build log | 102.4 kB |
| Network access | blocked |
| Maximum number of build targets | 10 |

                If your build fails because it hit one of these limits, please
                [open an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues/new/choose)
                to get them increased for your crate.
                Since our build agent has finite resources, we have to consider each case individually. However, there are a few general policies:

If your crate fails to build for a reason not listed here, you can rebuild it from [crates.io](https://crates.io) website as you can see below:

Or you can [file an issue](https://github.com/rust-lang/docs.rs/issues) if you think it's a **docs.rs** issue.

# Metadata

Source: https://docs.rs/about/metadata

You can customize docs.rs builds by defining `[package.metadata.docs.rs]`
		table in your crates' `Cargo.toml`.

The available configuration flags you can customize are:

```
[]
 = "test"
[]
# Features to pass to Cargo (default: [])
 = ["feature1", "feature2"]
# Whether to pass `--all-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Whether to pass `--no-default-features` to Cargo (default: false)
 = true
# Target to test build on, used as the default landing page (default: "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu")
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
 = "x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu"
# Targets to build (default: see below)
#
# Any target supported by rustup can be used.
#
# Default targets:
# - x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - aarch64-apple-darwin
# - x86_64-pc-windows-msvc
# - aarch64-unknown-linux-gnu
# - i686-pc-windows-msvc
#
# Set this to `[]` to only build the default target.
#
# If `default-target` is unset, the first element of `targets` is treated as the default target.
# Otherwise, these `targets` are built in addition to the default target.
# If both `default-target` and `targets` are unset,
#   all tier-one targets will be built and `x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu` will be used as the default target.
 = ["aarch64-apple-darwin", "x86_64-pc-windows-msvc"]
# If you want to instead add another target without overwriting the default ones:
 = ["i686-apple-darwin"]
# Additional `RUSTFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustc-arg"]
# Additional `RUSTDOCFLAGS` to set (default: [])
 = ["--example-rustdoc-arg"]
# List of command line arguments for `cargo`.
#
# These cannot be a subcommand, they may only be options.
 = ["-Z", "build-std"]
```

# Shorthand URLs

Source: https://docs.rs/about/redirections

Docs.rs uses semver to parse URLs. You can use this feature to access
            crates' documentation easily. Example of URL redirections for
            `clap` crate:

| URL | Redirects to documentation of |
|---|---|
| [docs.rs/clap](https://docs.rs/clap) | Latest version of clap |
| [docs.rs/clap::Command](https://docs.rs/clap::Command) | Latest version of clap, and search for "Command" within the crate |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2) | 2.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/~2.9](https://docs.rs/clap/%7E2.9) | 2.9.* version |
| [docs.rs/clap/2.9.3](https://docs.rs/clap/2.9.3) | 2.9.3 version (you don't need `=`unlike semver) |
| [docs.rs/clap/*](https://docs.rs/clap/*) | Latest version of this page (if it still exists). "latest" or "newest" work as well as `*`. |

# Download

Source: https://docs.rs/about/download

docs.rs stores the `rustdoc` output in a ZIP file.

                These archives can be used as a base for further processing of
                the documentation for offline readers like Dash or Zeal.
                **They are not directly usable for offline documentation.**

The download is possible for specific or semantic versions:

But also viaTo unpack the ZIP file you need any zip utility that supports PKZIP version 4.6 and BZIP2 & Deflate compression.

The archives will contain all the documentation HTML files for all targets and CSS/JS assets that are specific to the build. The default target will be found at the root, and other targets each in its own subfolder.

                Docs.rs is running rustdoc with `--static-root-path "/-/rustdoc.static/"`,
                which leads to all references to static assets breaking if they are not
                available under that path. Older builds used `--static-root-path "/"`, which
                means you will have to handle both.

                Since we're also adding `--emit=invocation-specific` to our build
                the archives will *not* contain any static assets that are specific to the
                toolchain. For now these will have to be downloaded file-by-file directly
                from docs.rs.

# Rustdoc JSON

Source: https://docs.rs/about/rustdoc-json

docs.rs builds & hosts the [ rustdoc JSON](https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustdoc/unstable-features.html#json-output) output.

This structured version of the documentation can be used for inspecting the docs and types of the crate in a programmatic way.

                The JSON file you're downloading might have been built with an older version of `rustdoc`
                so you might have to check the `format_version` attribute to determine how to parse the structure.
                The [ rustdoc-types](https://docs.rs/rustdoc-types/) crate helps with this.

**
                We started building rustdoc JSON on 2025-05-23. So any release before that won't have a download
                available until our rebuilds reached that release.
            **

                The download URLs can be generic or specific, depending on what you need. In case of rebuilds we
                also keep old format versions around. **Until we rebuilt all releases, we might return
                a `404 NOT FOUND` for some.**

By default we use `zstd` compression, which is more space efficient and faster to decompress. For more limited environments we also started supporting `gzip` compression. You can receive gzip by adding `.gz` to the given URL.

Here some URL examples you can use.

| URL | Redirects to JSON download of |
|---|---|
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json) | latest version, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json.gz) | latest version, default target, latest format-version, gzip compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/json/42) | latest version, default target, format-version 42 |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/~4/json.zst](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/%7E4/json.zst) | latest v4 via semver, default target, latest format-version, zstd compression |
| [https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json](https://docs.rs/crate/clap/latest/i686-pc-windows-msvc/json) | latest version, windows target, latest format-version |

### Create a new project

```
```
Generated structure:

```
myapp/
├── src/
│   ├── main.rs
│   ├── router.rs
│   ├── prelude.rs
│   ├── controller/
│   │   └── home.rs
│   ├── middleware/
│   ├── service/
│   │   ├── mod.rs        # services! container
│   │   └── user.rs
│   ├── schedule/
│   └── helper/
│       └── response.rs
├── config/
│   ├── config.default.toml
│   └── config.prod.toml
└── Cargo.toml
```
### Generate code (auto-register)

All generators automatically register into the appropriate files — zero manual wiring.

```
# Generate controller (alias: g c)
# → Creates src/controller/user.rs
# → Auto-registers in controller/mod.rs + router.rs
# Generate service (alias: g s)
# → Creates src/service/order.rs
# → Auto-registers in service/mod.rs (services! macro)
# Generate middleware (alias: g m)
# → Creates src/middleware/rate_limit.rs (Ctx + Next + ReqParts signature)
# → Auto-registers in middleware/mod.rs
# Generate schedule job (alias: g j)
# → Creates src/schedule/cleanup.rs
# → Auto-registers in schedule/mod.rs + main.rs (.schedule())
```
### Development server (hot reload)

```
```
Watches file changes, recompiles, and restarts automatically.

```
```
## Configuration

Each middleware/feature manages its own config section:

```
# config/config.default.toml
[]
 = 3000
[]
 = true
 = ["*"]
[]
 = true
[]
 = true
 = false
```
Rule: **has section +  enable = true = on.** No section or

`enable = false` = off.## Links

# aerocontext_leidos - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/aerocontext-leidos/0.4.5/aerocontext_leidos/

## Expand description

[ aerocontext_core::WeatherBriefingProvider](https://docs.rs/aerocontext-core/0.4.5/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/aerocontext_core/weather/trait.WeatherBriefingProvider.html),

[,](https://docs.rs/aerocontext-core/0.4.5/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/aerocontext_core/notam/trait.NotamProvider.html)

`aerocontext_core::NotamProvider`[, and](https://docs.rs/aerocontext-core/0.4.5/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/aerocontext_core/tfr/trait.TfrProvider.html)

`aerocontext_core::TfrProvider`[adapter for the Leidos Flight Service (1800wxbrief) Pilot Web Service.](https://docs.rs/aerocontext-core/0.4.5/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/aerocontext_core/route_alert/trait.RouteAlertProvider.html)

`aerocontext_core::RouteAlertProvider`Speaks the FFSP REST API (form-urlencoded `POST` to
`FP/areaBriefing` / `FP/routeBriefing`), returning
a `SIMPLE` briefing for a circular area around a fix or coordinate,
authenticated with pre-emptive HTTP Basic vendor credentials. Requests
are sent with `notABriefing=true` — data retrieval only, with no pilot
association and no historical retention. NOTAMs are extracted from the same
`SIMPLE` narrative as low-fidelity records for cross-source reconciliation.
[ LeidosClient::area_briefing_pdf](https://docs.rs/struct.LeidosClient.html#method.area_briefing_pdf) requests the same area as an NGBv2
briefing (

`briefingResultFormat=PDF`) and returns the vendor-composed
standard briefing as decoded PDF bytes.
Recorded pilot briefings (`webUserName` + `aircraftIdentifier` +
service-provider authorization) are a future extension.Independent, unofficial adapter (test server only) — not affiliated with or endorsed by Leidos or the FAA.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- Leidos FFSP Pilot Web Service client.

- Configuration for `LeidosClient`

- Leidos evaluation/test (ffspelabs) REST base. Resource paths
(`FP/areaBriefing`,`FP/routeBriefing`, …) are appended to it. This is the only endpoint this adapter targets; production 1800wxbrief is not wired.

# aerocontext_nms - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/aerocontext-nms/0.4.5/aerocontext_nms/

## Expand description

FAA NOTAM Management System (NMS-API) NOTAM source for `aerocontext-core`.

[ NmsClient](https://docs.rs/struct.NmsClient.html) implements

[: it authenticates with OAuth2](https://docs.rs/aerocontext-core/0.4.5/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/aerocontext_core/notam/trait.NotamProvider.html)

`aerocontext_core::NotamProvider``client_credentials` (an FAA-issued client id and
secret, env-only and never persisted), queries `/v1/notams` in GeoJSON, and
maps each NOTAM onto a provider-neutral [. It “packs what the vendor has”; assembling and cross-checking against other sources is](https://docs.rs/aerocontext-core/0.4.5/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/aerocontext_core/notam/struct.NotamRecord.html)

`aerocontext_core::NotamRecord`[’s job, not this crate’s.](https://docs.rs/aerocontext-core/0.4.5/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/aerocontext_core/notam/reconcile/fn.reconcile.html)

`aerocontext_core::reconcile`Defaults target the FAA **staging** environment; production is two env
overrides ([ BASE_URL_ENV](https://docs.rs/constant.BASE_URL_ENV.html) /

[), not a code change.](https://docs.rs/constant.AUTH_URL_ENV.html)

`AUTH_URL_ENV`Independent, unofficial adapter — not affiliated with or endorsed by the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration.

# aerocontext_awc - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/aerocontext-awc/0.4.5/aerocontext_awc/

## Expand description

[ aerocontext_core::WeatherBriefingProvider](https://docs.rs/aerocontext-core/0.4.5/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/aerocontext_core/weather/trait.WeatherBriefingProvider.html) adapter for the
aviationweather.gov Data API.

The Data API is product-oriented: an area briefing fans out over the
per-product endpoints (`metar`, `taf`, `pirep`, `airsigmet`) under
`https://aviationweather.gov/api/data/` and normalizes the JSON
responses into [ aerocontext_core::Product](https://docs.rs/aerocontext-core/0.4.5/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/aerocontext_core/model/struct.Product.html)s. No authentication is
required, but AWC asks clients to send a custom

`User-Agent`.Independent, unofficial adapter — not affiliated with or endorsed by the NOAA/NWS Aviation Weather Center.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [AwcClient](https://docs.rs/struct.AwcClient.html)
- aviationweather.gov Data API client.
- [AwcConfig](https://docs.rs/struct.AwcConfig.html)
- Configuration for `AwcClient`
- [Route](https://docs.rs/struct.RouteFanout.html)- Fanout
- The fan-out shape of an AWC route briefing: `segments * kinds`upstream requests, one per corridor bounding box per product kind.

## Enums[§](https://docs.rs#enums)

- [Config](https://docs.rs/enum.ConfigError.html)- Error
- Failure constructing an `AwcClient`

## Constants[§](https://docs.rs#constants)

- [DEFAULT_](https://docs.rs/constant.DEFAULT_BASE_URL.html)- BASE_ - URL
- Production base URL of the Data API.

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [route_](https://docs.rs/fn.route_fanout.html)- fanout
- Predict the fan-out `AwcClient::route_briefing``request`—`segments * kinds`sequential upstream requests. Lets a caller (e.g. an agent-facing tool fed untrusted input) refuse an oversized request before issuing a single call.

# aerocontext_planning - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/aerocontext-planning/0.4.5/aerocontext_planning/

## Expand description

Flight-route planning: the single engine that turns a route or a flight plan into usable geometry.

Every frontend — the `aerocontext` CLI, the MCP `route_brief` tool, a
future GUI or iOS app — composes this crate rather than reimplementing
any of it. The hub is the [ flightplan::FlightPlan](https://docs.rs/flightplan/struct.FlightPlan.html) domain model;
Garmin

`.fpl` is one *codec*(inside

[), not the privileged format, so other formats slot in beside it without touching planning logic.](https://docs.rs/flightplan/index.html)

`flightplan`The pieces:

- `flightplan`- `FlightPlan`model and its- `.fpl`codec.
- `route`- `NavDataSnapshot`
- `corridor`
- `crosssection`- `AircraftProfile`

This crate consumes the cycle-stamped snapshot that `aerocontext-navdata`
produces; it never fetches or distributes data itself.

# line_wrap - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/line-wrap/0.2.0/target-redirect/line_wrap/

## Expand description

Efficiently insert line endings.

If you have a buffer full of data and want to insert any sort of regularly-spaced separator,
this will do it with a minimum of data copying. Commonly, this is to insert `\n` (see `lf()`) or `\r\n` (`crlf()`), but
any byte sequence can be used.

- Pick a line ending. For single byte separators, see `ByteLineEnding`, or for two bytes,`TwoByteLineEnding`. For arbitrary byte slices, use`SliceLineEnding`.
- Call `line_wrap`.
- Your data has been rearranged in place with the specified line ending inserted.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use line_wrap::*;
// suppose we have 80 bytes of data in a buffer and we want to wrap as per MIME.
// Buffer is large enough to hold line endings.
let mut data = vec![0; 82];
assert_eq!(2, line_wrap(&mut data, 80, 76, &crlf()));
// first line of zeroes
let mut expected_data = vec![0; 76];
// line ending
expected_data.extend_from_slice(b"\r\n");
// next line
expected_data.extend_from_slice(&[0, 0, 0, 0]);
assert_eq!(expected_data, data);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#performance)Performance

On an i7 6850k:

- 10 byte input, 1 byte line length takes ~60ns (~160MiB/s)
- 100 byte input, 10 byte lines takes ~60ns (~1.6GiB/s)
- Startup costs dominate at these small lengths

- 1,000 byte input, 100 byte lines takes ~65ns (~15GiB/s)
- 10,000 byte input, 100 byte lines takes ~550ns (~17GiB/s)
- In general, `SliceLineEncoding`is about 75% the speed of the fixed-length impls.

Naturally, try `cargo +nightly bench` on your hardware to get more representative data.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Byte](https://docs.rs/struct.ByteLineEnding.html)- Line - Ending
- A single byte line ending.
- [Slice](https://docs.rs/struct.SliceLineEnding.html)- Line - Ending
- A byte slice line ending.
- [TwoByte](https://docs.rs/struct.TwoByteLineEnding.html)- Line - Ending
- A double byte line ending.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Line](https://docs.rs/trait.LineEnding.html)- Ending
- Writes line endings.

[196](https://docs.rs#196)
[197](https://docs.rs#197)/// Insert line endings into the input.
[198](https://docs.rs#198)///
[199](https://docs.rs#199)/// Endings are inserted after each complete line, except the last line, even if the last line takes
[200](https://docs.rs#200)/// up the full line width.
[201](https://docs.rs#201)///
[202](https://docs.rs#202)/// - `buf` must be large enough to handle the increased size after endings are inserted. In other
[203](https://docs.rs#203)/// words, `buf.len() >= input_len / line_len * line_ending.len()`.
[204](https://docs.rs#204)/// - `input_len` is the length of the unwrapped  in `buf`.
[205](https://docs.rs#205)/// - `line_len` is the desired line width without line ending characters.
[206](https://docs.rs#206)///
[207](https://docs.rs#207)/// Returns the number of line ending bytes added.
[208](https://docs.rs#208)///
[209](https://docs.rs#209)/// # Panics
[210](https://docs.rs#210)///
[211](https://docs.rs#211)/// - When `buf` is too small to contain the original input and its new line endings
[212](https://docs.rs#212)pub fn line_wrap<L: LineEnding>(
[213](https://docs.rs#213)    buf: &mut [u8],
[214](https://docs.rs#214)    input_len: usize,
[215](https://docs.rs#215)    line_len: usize,
[216](https://docs.rs#216)    line_ending: &L,
[217](https://docs.rs#217)) -> usize {
[218](https://docs.rs#218)    if input_len <= line_len {
[219](https://docs.rs#219)        return 0;
[220](https://docs.rs#220)    }
[221](https://docs.rs#221)
[222](https://docs.rs#222)    let line_ending_len = line_ending.len();
[223](https://docs.rs#223)    let line_wrap_params = line_wrap_parameters(input_len, line_len, line_ending_len);
[224](https://docs.rs#224)
[225](https://docs.rs#225)    // ptr.offset() is undefined if it wraps, and there is no checked_offset(). However, because
[226](https://docs.rs#226)    // we perform this check up front to make sure we have enough capacity, we know that none of
[227](https://docs.rs#227)    // the subsequent pointer operations (assuming they implement the desired behavior of course!)
[228](https://docs.rs#228)    // will overflow.
[229](https://docs.rs#229)    assert!(
[230](https://docs.rs#230)        buf.len() >= line_wrap_params.total_len,
[231](https://docs.rs#231)        "Buffer must be able to hold encoded data after line wrapping"
[232](https://docs.rs#232)    );
[233](https://docs.rs#233)
[234](https://docs.rs#234)    // Move the last line, either partial or full, by itself as it does not have a line ending
[235](https://docs.rs#235)    // afterwards
[236](https://docs.rs#236)    let last_line_start = input_len
[237](https://docs.rs#237)        .checked_sub(line_wrap_params.last_line_len)
[238](https://docs.rs#238)        .expect("Last line start index underflow");
[239](https://docs.rs#239)    // last line starts immediately after all the wrapped full lines
[240](https://docs.rs#240)    let new_line_start = line_wrap_params.total_full_wrapped_lines_len;
[241](https://docs.rs#241)
[242](https://docs.rs#242)    buf.copy_within(
[243](https://docs.rs#243)        last_line_start..(last_line_start + line_wrap_params.last_line_len),
[244](https://docs.rs#244)        new_line_start,
[245](https://docs.rs#245)    );
[246](https://docs.rs#246)
[247](https://docs.rs#247)    let mut total_line_ending_bytes = 0;
[248](https://docs.rs#248)
[249](https://docs.rs#249)    // initialize so that the initial decrement will set them correctly
[250](https://docs.rs#250)    let mut old_line_start = last_line_start;
[251](https://docs.rs#251)    let mut new_line_start = line_wrap_params.total_full_wrapped_lines_len;
[252](https://docs.rs#252)
[253](https://docs.rs#253)    // handle the full lines
[254](https://docs.rs#254)    for _ in 0..line_wrap_params.lines_with_endings {
[255](https://docs.rs#255)        // the index after the end of the line ending we're about to write is the start of the next
[256](https://docs.rs#256)        // line
[257](https://docs.rs#257)        let end_of_line_ending = new_line_start;
[258](https://docs.rs#258)        let start_of_line_ending = end_of_line_ending
[259](https://docs.rs#259)            .checked_sub(line_ending_len.get())
[260](https://docs.rs#260)            .expect("Line ending start index underflow");
[261](https://docs.rs#261)
[262](https://docs.rs#262)        // doesn't underflow because it's decremented `line_wrap_params.lines_with_endings` times
[263](https://docs.rs#263)        old_line_start = old_line_start
[264](https://docs.rs#264)            .checked_sub(line_len)
[265](https://docs.rs#265)            .expect("Old line start index underflow");
[266](https://docs.rs#266)        new_line_start = new_line_start
[267](https://docs.rs#267)            .checked_sub(line_wrap_params.line_with_ending_len)
[268](https://docs.rs#268)            .expect("New line start index underflow");
[269](https://docs.rs#269)
[270](https://docs.rs#270)        buf.copy_within(old_line_start..old_line_start + line_len, new_line_start);
[271](https://docs.rs#271)
[272](https://docs.rs#272)        line_ending.write_ending(&mut buf[start_of_line_ending..end_of_line_ending]);
[273](https://docs.rs#273)        total_line_ending_bytes += line_ending_len.get();
[274](https://docs.rs#274)    }
[275](https://docs.rs#275)
[276](https://docs.rs#276)    assert_eq!(
[277](https://docs.rs#277)        line_wrap_params.total_line_endings_len,
[278](https://docs.rs#278)        total_line_ending_bytes
[279](https://docs.rs#279)    );
[280](https://docs.rs#280)
[281](https://docs.rs#281)    total_line_ending_bytes
[282](https://docs.rs#282)}
[283](https://docs.rs#283)
[284](https://docs.rs#284)#[derive(Debug, PartialEq)]
[285](https://docs.rs#285)struct LineWrapParameters {
[286](https://docs.rs#286)    line_with_ending_len: usize,
[287](https://docs.rs#287)    // number of lines that need an ending
[288](https://docs.rs#288)    lines_with_endings: usize,
[289](https://docs.rs#289)    // length of last line (which never needs an ending)
[290](https://docs.rs#290)    last_line_len: usize,
[291](https://docs.rs#291)    // length of lines that need an ending (which are always full lines), with their endings
[292](https://docs.rs#292)    total_full_wrapped_lines_len: usize,
[293](https://docs.rs#293)    // length of all lines, including endings for the ones that need them
[294](https://docs.rs#294)    total_len: usize,
[295](https://docs.rs#295)    // length of the line endings only
[296](https://docs.rs#296)    total_line_endings_len: usize,
[297](https://docs.rs#297)}
[298](https://docs.rs#298)
[299](https://docs.rs#299)/// Calculations about how many lines we'll get for a given line length, line ending, etc.
[300](https://docs.rs#300)/// This assumes that the last line will not get an ending, even if it is the full line length.
[301](https://docs.rs#301)// Inlining improves short input single-byte by 25%.
[302](https://docs.rs#302)#[inline]
[303](https://docs.rs#303)fn line_wrap_parameters(
[304](https://docs.rs#304)    input_len: usize,
[305](https://docs.rs#305)    line_len: usize,
[306](https://docs.rs#306)    line_ending_len: NonZeroUsize,
[307](https://docs.rs#307)) -> LineWrapParameters {
[308](https://docs.rs#308)    let line_with_ending_len = line_len
[309](https://docs.rs#309)        .checked_add(line_ending_len.get())
[310](https://docs.rs#310)        .expect("Line length with ending exceeds usize");
[311](https://docs.rs#311)
[312](https://docs.rs#312)    if input_len <= line_len {
[313](https://docs.rs#313)        // no wrapping needed
[314](https://docs.rs#314)        return LineWrapParameters {
[315](https://docs.rs#315)            line_with_ending_len,
[316](https://docs.rs#316)            lines_with_endings: 0,
[317](https://docs.rs#317)            last_line_len: input_len,
[318](https://docs.rs#318)            total_full_wrapped_lines_len: 0,
[319](https://docs.rs#319)            total_len: input_len,
[320](https://docs.rs#320)            total_line_endings_len: 0,
[321](https://docs.rs#321)        };
[322](https://docs.rs#322)    };
[323](https://docs.rs#323)
[324](https://docs.rs#324)    // lines_with_endings > 0, last_line_len > 0
[325](https://docs.rs#325)    let (lines_with_endings, last_line_len) = if input_len % line_len > 0 {
[326](https://docs.rs#326)        // Every full line has an ending since there is a partial line at the end
[327](https://docs.rs#327)        (input_len / line_len, input_len % line_len)
[328](https://docs.rs#328)    } else {
[329](https://docs.rs#329)        // Every line is a full line, but no trailing ending.
[330](https://docs.rs#330)        // Subtraction will not underflow since we know input_len > line_len.
[331](https://docs.rs#331)        (input_len / line_len - 1, line_len)
[332](https://docs.rs#332)    };
[333](https://docs.rs#333)
[334](https://docs.rs#334)    // Should we expose exceeding usize via Result to be kind to 16-bit users? Or is that
[335](https://docs.rs#335)    // always going to be a panic anyway in practice?
[336](https://docs.rs#336)
[337](https://docs.rs#337)    // length of just the full lines with line endings
[338](https://docs.rs#338)    let total_full_wrapped_lines_len = lines_with_endings
[339](https://docs.rs#339)        .checked_mul(line_with_ending_len)
[340](https://docs.rs#340)        .expect("Full lines with endings length exceeds usize");
[341](https://docs.rs#341)    // all lines with appropriate endings, including the last line
[342](https://docs.rs#342)    let total_len = total_full_wrapped_lines_len
[343](https://docs.rs#343)        .checked_add(last_line_len)
[344](https://docs.rs#344)        .expect("All lines with endings length exceeds usize");
[345](https://docs.rs#345)    let total_line_endings_len = lines_with_endings
[346](https://docs.rs#346)        .checked_mul(line_ending_len.get())
[347](https://docs.rs#347)        .expect("Total line endings length exceeds usize");
[348](https://docs.rs#348)
[349](https://docs.rs#349)    LineWrapParameters {
[350](https://docs.rs#350)        line_with_ending_len,
[351](https://docs.rs#351)        lines_with_endings,
[352](https://docs.rs#352)        last_line_len,
[353](https://docs.rs#353)        total_full_wrapped_lines_len,
[354](https://docs.rs#354)        total_len,
[355](https://docs.rs#355)        total_line_endings_len,
[356](https://docs.rs#356)    }
[357](https://docs.rs#357)}
[358](https://docs.rs#358)
[359](https://docs.rs#359)#[cfg(test)]
[360](https://docs.rs#360)mod tests;

# line_wrap in line_wrap - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/line-wrap/0.2.0/line_wrap/fn.line_wrap.html

`pub fn line_wrap<L: `[LineEnding](https://docs.rs/trait.LineEnding.html)>(
    buf: &mut [[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.u8.html)],
    input_len: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.usize.html),
    line_len: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.usize.html),
    line_ending: [&L](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.reference.html),
) -> [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/primitive.usize.html)## Expand description

Insert line endings into the input.

Endings are inserted after each complete line, except the last line, even if the last line takes up the full line width.

- `buf`must be large enough to handle the increased size after endings are inserted. In other words,- `buf.len() >= input_len / line_len * line_ending.len()`.
- `input_len`is the length of the unwrapped in- `buf`.
- `line_len`is the desired line width without line ending characters.

Returns the number of line ending bytes added.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics)Panics

- When `buf`is too small to contain the original input and its new line endings

# line_wrap - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/line-wrap/latest/line_wrap/

## Expand description

Efficiently insert line endings.

If you have a buffer full of data and want to insert any sort of regularly-spaced separator,
this will do it with a minimum of data copying. Commonly, this is to insert `\n` (see `lf()`) or `\r\n` (`crlf()`), but
any byte sequence can be used.

- Pick a line ending. For single byte separators, see `ByteLineEnding`, or for two bytes,`TwoByteLineEnding`. For arbitrary byte slices, use`SliceLineEnding`.
- Call `line_wrap`.
- Your data has been rearranged in place with the specified line ending inserted.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
use line_wrap::*;
// suppose we have 80 bytes of data in a buffer and we want to wrap as per MIME.
// Buffer is large enough to hold line endings.
let mut data = vec![0; 82];
assert_eq!(2, line_wrap(&mut data, 80, 76, &crlf()));
// first line of zeroes
let mut expected_data = vec![0; 76];
// line ending
expected_data.extend_from_slice(b"\r\n");
// next line
expected_data.extend_from_slice(&[0, 0, 0, 0]);
assert_eq!(expected_data, data);
```
[§](https://docs.rs#performance)Performance

On an i7 6850k:

- 10 byte input, 1 byte line length takes ~60ns (~160MiB/s)
- 100 byte input, 10 byte lines takes ~60ns (~1.6GiB/s)
- Startup costs dominate at these small lengths

- 1,000 byte input, 100 byte lines takes ~65ns (~15GiB/s)
- 10,000 byte input, 100 byte lines takes ~550ns (~17GiB/s)
- In general, `SliceLineEncoding`is about 75% the speed of the fixed-length impls.

Naturally, try `cargo +nightly bench` on your hardware to get more representative data.

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- [Byte](https://docs.rs/struct.ByteLineEnding.html)- Line - Ending
- A single byte line ending.
- [Slice](https://docs.rs/struct.SliceLineEnding.html)- Line - Ending
- A byte slice line ending.
- [TwoByte](https://docs.rs/struct.TwoByteLineEnding.html)- Line - Ending
- A double byte line ending.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Line](https://docs.rs/trait.LineEnding.html)- Ending
- Writes line endings.

# rand 0.8.6 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rand/^0.8.5

# Rand

A Rust library for random number generation, featuring:

- Easy random value generation and usage via the `Rng``SliceRandom``IteratorRandom`
- Secure seeding via the `getrandom`crate`thread_rng`
- A modular design built over `rand_core`[see the book](https://rust-random.github.io/book/crates.html))
- Fast implementations of the best-in-class [cryptographic](https://rust-random.github.io/book/guide-rngs.html#cryptographically-secure-pseudo-random-number-generators-csprngs)and[non-cryptographic](https://rust-random.github.io/book/guide-rngs.html#basic-pseudo-random-number-generators-prngs)generators
- A flexible `distributions`
- Samplers for a large number of random number distributions via our own
`rand_distr``statrs`
- [Portably reproducible output](https://rust-random.github.io/book/portability.html)
- `#[no_std]`compatibility (partial)
- *Many*performance optimisations

It's also worth pointing out what `rand` *is not*:

- Small. Most low-level crates are small, but the higher-level `rand`and`rand_distr`each contain a lot of functionality.
- Simple (implementation). We have a strong focus on correctness, speed and flexibility, but
not simplicity. If you prefer a small-and-simple library, there are
alternatives including [fastrand](https://crates.io/crates/fastrand)and[oorandom](https://crates.io/crates/oorandom).
- Slow. We take performance seriously, with considerations also for set-up time of new distributions, commonly-used parameters, and parameters of the current sampler.

Documentation:

## Usage

Add this to your `Cargo.toml`:

```
[]
 = "0.8.4"
```
To get started using Rand, see [The Book](https://rust-random.github.io/book).

## Versions

Rand is *mature* (suitable for general usage, with infrequent breaking releases
which minimise breakage) but not yet at 1.0. We maintain compatibility with
pinned versions of the Rust compiler (see below).

Current Rand versions are:

- Version 0.7 was released in June 2019, moving most non-uniform distributions
to an external crate, moving `from_entropy`to`SeedableRng`, and many small changes and fixes.
- Version 0.8 was released in December 2020 with many small changes.

A detailed [changelog](https://docs.rs/CHANGELOG.md) is available for releases.

When upgrading to the next minor series (especially 0.4 → 0.5), we recommend
reading the [Upgrade Guide](https://rust-random.github.io/book/update.html).

Rand has not yet reached 1.0 implying some breaking changes may arrive in the
future ([SemVer](https://semver.org/) allows each 0.x.0 release to include
breaking changes), but is considered *mature*: breaking changes are minimised
and breaking releases are infrequent.

Rand libs have inter-dependencies and make use of the
[semver trick](https://github.com/dtolnay/semver-trick/) in order to make traits
compatible across crate versions. (This is especially important for `RngCore`
and `SeedableRng`.) A few crate releases are thus compatibility shims,
depending on the *next* lib version (e.g. `rand_core` versions `0.2.2` and
`0.3.1`). This means, for example, that `rand_core_0_4_0::SeedableRng` and
`rand_core_0_3_0::SeedableRng` are distinct, incompatible traits, which can
cause build errors. Usually, running `cargo update` is enough to fix any issues.

### Yanked versions

Some versions of Rand crates have been yanked ("unreleased"). Where this occurs,
the crate's CHANGELOG *should* be updated with a rationale, and a search on the
issue tracker with the keyword `yank` *should* uncover the motivation.

### Rust version requirements

Since version 0.8, Rand requires **Rustc version 1.36 or greater**.
Rand 0.7 requires Rustc 1.32 or greater while versions 0.5 require Rustc 1.22 or
greater, and 0.4 and 0.3 (since approx. June 2017) require Rustc version 1.15 or
greater. Subsets of the Rand code may work with older Rust versions, but this is
not supported.

Continuous Integration (CI) will always test the minimum supported Rustc version (the MSRV). The current policy is that this can be updated in any Rand release if required, but the change must be noted in the changelog.

## Crate Features

Rand is built with these features enabled by default:

- `std`enables functionality dependent on the- `std`lib
- `alloc`(implied by- `std`) enables functionality requiring an allocator
- `getrandom`(implied by- `std`) is an optional dependency providing the code behind- `rngs::OsRng`
- `std_rng`enables inclusion of- `StdRng`,- `thread_rng`and- `random`(the latter two- *also*require that- `std`be enabled)

Additionally, these features configure Rand:

- `small_rng`enables inclusion of the- `SmallRng`PRNG
- `nightly`enables some optimizations requiring nightly Rust
- `min_const_gen`enables generating random arrays of any size using min-const-generics, requiring Rust ≥ 1.51.

Note that nightly features are not stable and therefore not all library and
compiler versions will be compatible. This is especially true of Rand's
experimental `simd_support` feature, which was dropped by version 0.8.6 of Rand.

Rand supports limited functionality in `no_std` mode (enabled via
`default-features = false`). In this case, `OsRng` and `from_entropy` are
unavailable (unless `getrandom` is enabled), large parts of `seq` are
unavailable (unless `alloc` is enabled), and `thread_rng` and `random` are
unavailable.

### WASM support

The WASM target `wasm32-unknown-unknown` is not *automatically* supported by
`rand` or `getrandom`. To solve this, either use a different target such as
`wasm32-wasi` or add a direct dependency on `getrandom` with the `js` feature
(if the target supports JavaScript). See
[getrandom#WebAssembly support](https://docs.rs/getrandom/latest/getrandom/#webassembly-support).

# rand 0.8.6 - Docs.rs

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rand/0.8.6

# Rand

A Rust library for random number generation, featuring:

- Easy random value generation and usage via the `Rng``SliceRandom``IteratorRandom`
- Secure seeding via the `getrandom`crate`thread_rng`
- A modular design built over `rand_core`[see the book](https://rust-random.github.io/book/crates.html))
- Fast implementations of the best-in-class [cryptographic](https://rust-random.github.io/book/guide-rngs.html#cryptographically-secure-pseudo-random-number-generators-csprngs)and[non-cryptographic](https://rust-random.github.io/book/guide-rngs.html#basic-pseudo-random-number-generators-prngs)generators
- A flexible `distributions`
- Samplers for a large number of random number distributions via our own
`rand_distr``statrs`
- [Portably reproducible output](https://rust-random.github.io/book/portability.html)
- `#[no_std]`compatibility (partial)
- *Many*performance optimisations

It's also worth pointing out what `rand` *is not*:

- Small. Most low-level crates are small, but the higher-level `rand`and`rand_distr`each contain a lot of functionality.
- Simple (implementation). We have a strong focus on correctness, speed and flexibility, but
not simplicity. If you prefer a small-and-simple library, there are
alternatives including [fastrand](https://crates.io/crates/fastrand)and[oorandom](https://crates.io/crates/oorandom).
- Slow. We take performance seriously, with considerations also for set-up time of new distributions, commonly-used parameters, and parameters of the current sampler.

Documentation:

# serde - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/serde/^1.0.103/

## Expand description

[§](https://docs.rs#serde)Serde

Serde is a framework for * ser*ializing and

*serializing Rust data structures efficiently and generically.*

**de**The Serde ecosystem consists of data structures that know how to serialize and deserialize themselves along with data formats that know how to serialize and deserialize other things. Serde provides the layer by which these two groups interact with each other, allowing any supported data structure to be serialized and deserialized using any supported data format.

See the Serde website [https://serde.rs](https://serde.rs) for additional documentation and
usage examples.

[§](https://docs.rs#design)Design

Where many other languages rely on runtime reflection for serializing data,
Serde is instead built on Rust’s powerful trait system. A data structure
that knows how to serialize and deserialize itself is one that implements
Serde’s `Serialize` and `Deserialize` traits (or uses Serde’s derive
attribute to automatically generate implementations at compile time). This
avoids any overhead of reflection or runtime type information. In fact in
many situations the interaction between data structure and data format can
be completely optimized away by the Rust compiler, leaving Serde
serialization to perform the same speed as a handwritten serializer for the
specific selection of data structure and data format.

[§](https://docs.rs#data-formats)Data formats

The following is a partial list of data formats that have been implemented for Serde by the community.

- [JSON](https://github.com/serde-rs/json), the ubiquitous JavaScript Object Notation used by many HTTP APIs.
- [Postcard](https://github.com/jamesmunns/postcard), a no_std and embedded-systems friendly compact binary format.
- [CBOR](https://github.com/enarx/ciborium), a Concise Binary Object Representation designed for small message size without the need for version negotiation.
- [YAML](https://github.com/dtolnay/serde-yaml), a self-proclaimed human-friendly configuration language that ain’t markup language.
- [MessagePack](https://github.com/3Hren/msgpack-rust), an efficient binary format that resembles a compact JSON.
- [TOML](https://docs.rs/toml), a minimal configuration format used by- [Cargo](https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/reference/manifest.html).
- [Pickle](https://github.com/birkenfeld/serde-pickle), a format common in the Python world.
- [RON](https://github.com/ron-rs/ron), a Rusty Object Notation.
- [BSON](https://github.com/mongodb/bson-rust), the data storage and network transfer format used by MongoDB.
- [Avro](https://docs.rs/apache-avro), a binary format used within Apache Hadoop, with support for schema definition.
- [JSON5](https://github.com/callum-oakley/json5-rs), a superset of JSON including some productions from ES5.
- [URL](https://docs.rs/serde_qs)query strings, in the x-www-form-urlencoded format.
- [Starlark](https://github.com/dtolnay/serde-starlark), the format used for describing build targets by the Bazel and Buck build systems.- *(serialization only)*
- [Envy](https://github.com/softprops/envy), a way to deserialize environment variables into Rust structs.- *(deserialization only)*
- [Envy Store](https://github.com/softprops/envy-store), a way to deserialize- [AWS Parameter Store](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/systems-manager/latest/userguide/systems-manager-parameter-store.html)parameters into Rust structs.- *(deserialization only)*
- [S-expressions](https://github.com/rotty/lexpr-rs), the textual representation of code and data used by the Lisp language family.
- [D-Bus](https://docs.rs/zvariant)’s binary wire format.
- [FlexBuffers](https://github.com/google/flatbuffers/tree/master/rust/flexbuffers), the schemaless cousin of Google’s FlatBuffers zero-copy serialization format.
- [Bencode](https://github.com/P3KI/bendy), a simple binary format used in the BitTorrent protocol.
- [Token streams](https://github.com/oxidecomputer/serde_tokenstream), for processing Rust procedural macro input.- *(deserialization only)*
- [DynamoDB Items](https://docs.rs/serde_dynamo), the format used by- [rusoto_dynamodb](https://docs.rs/rusoto_dynamodb)to transfer data to and from DynamoDB.
- [Hjson](https://github.com/Canop/deser-hjson), a syntax extension to JSON designed around human reading and editing.- *(deserialization only)*
- [CSV](https://docs.rs/csv), Comma-separated values is a tabular text file format.

## Modules[§](https://docs.rs#modules)

- [de](https://docs.rs/de/index.html)
- Generic data structure deserialization framework.
- [ser](https://docs.rs/ser/index.html)
- Generic data structure serialization framework.

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- A **data structure**that can be deserialized from any data format supported by Serde.
- [Deserializer](https://docs.rs/trait.Deserializer.html)
- A **data format**that can deserialize any data structure supported by Serde.
- [Serialize](https://docs.rs/trait.Serialize.html)
- A **data structure**that can be serialized into any data format supported by Serde.
- [Serializer](https://docs.rs/trait.Serializer.html)
- A **data format**that can serialize any data structure supported by Serde.

# bincode - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/bincode/^1.2.1/

## Expand description

Bincode is a crate for encoding and decoding using a tiny binary serialization strategy. Using it, you can easily go from having an object in memory, quickly serialize it to bytes, and then deserialize it back just as fast!

[§](https://docs.rs#using-basic-functions)Using Basic Functions

[ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

```
fn main() {
    // The object that we will serialize.
    let target: Option<String>  = Some("hello world".to_string());
    let encoded: Vec<u8> = bincode::serialize(&target).unwrap();
    let decoded: Option<String> = bincode::deserialize(&encoded[..]).unwrap();
    assert_eq!(target, decoded);
}
```
[§](https://docs.rs#128bit-numbers)128bit numbers

Support for `i128` and `u128` is automatically enabled on Rust toolchains
greater than or equal to `1.26.0` and disabled for targets which do not support it

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use config::`- [Config](https://docs.rs/config/struct.Config.html);- Deprecated
- `pub use config::`- [DefaultOptions](https://docs.rs/config/struct.DefaultOptions.html);
- `pub use config::`- [Options](https://docs.rs/config/trait.Options.html);
- `pub use de::read::`- [BincodeRead](https://docs.rs/de/read/trait.BincodeRead.html);
- `pub use de::`- [Deserializer](https://docs.rs/de/struct.Deserializer.html);

- [de](https://docs.rs/de/index.html)
- Deserialize bincode data to a Rust data structure.

- Deserializes a slice of bytes into an instance of `T`using the default configuration.

- Deserializes an object from a custom `BincodeRead`er using the default configuration. It is highly recommended to use`deserialize_from`unless you need to implement`BincodeRead`for performance reasons.

# rand_pcg - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand_pcg/^0.3.0/

## Expand description

The PCG random number generators.

This is a native Rust implementation of a small selection of PCG generators. The primary goal of this crate is simple, minimal, well-tested code; in other words it is explicitly not a goal to re-implement all of PCG.

This crate provides:

- `Pcg32`aka- `Lcg64Xsh32`, officially known as- `pcg32`, a general purpose RNG. This is a good choice on both 32-bit and 64-bit CPUs (for 32-bit output).
- `Pcg64`aka- `Lcg128Xsl64`, officially known as- `pcg64`, a general purpose RNG. This is a good choice on 64-bit CPUs.
- `Pcg64Mcg`aka- `Mcg128Xsl64`, officially known as- `pcg64_fast`, a general purpose RNG using 128-bit multiplications. This has poor performance on 32-bit CPUs but is a good choice on 64-bit CPUs for both 32-bit and 64-bit output.

Both of these use 16 bytes of state and 128-bit seeds, and are considered value-stable (i.e. any change affecting the output given a fixed seed would be considered a breaking change to the crate).

## Structs[§](https://docs.rs#structs)

- A PCG random number generator (XSH RR 64/32 (LCG) variant).
- A PCG random number generator (XSL RR 128/64 (LCG) variant).
- A PCG random number generator (XSL 128/64 (MCG) variant).

# rand - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/crate/rand/latest/target-redirect/rand/

## Expand description

Random-number generators and samplers

[§](https://docs.rs#quick-start)Quick Start

```
// rand::random() supports many common types:
println!("Uniform i8 sample: {}", match rand::random() {
    0i8 => "zero",
    i if i > 0 => "positive",
    _ => "negative",
});
// Ranged sampling:
use std::f32::consts::PI;
println!("Angle: {} degrees", rand::random_range(-PI..PI));
```
See also [The Book: Quick Start](https://rust-random.github.io/book/quick-start.html).

## Re-exports[§](https://docs.rs#reexports)

- `pub use`- [rand_core](https://docs.rs/rand_core/0.10.1/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/rand_core/index.html);

- Generating random samples from probability distributions
- [prelude](https://docs.rs/prelude/index.html)
- Convenience re-export of common members
- [rngs](https://docs.rs/rngs/index.html)
- Random number generators and adapters
- [seq](https://docs.rs/seq/index.html)
- Sequence-related functionality

## Traits[§](https://docs.rs#traits)

- [Crypto](https://docs.rs/trait.CryptoRng.html)- Rng
- A marker trait for securely unpredictable infallible RNGs

- Support filling a slice with random data
- [Rng](https://docs.rs/trait.Rng.html)
- Trait for infallible random number generators

- User-level interface for RNGs
- [Seedable](https://docs.rs/trait.SeedableRng.html)- Rng
- A random number generator that can be explicitly seeded.
- [TryCrypto](https://docs.rs/trait.TryCryptoRng.html)- Rng
- A marker trait over `TryRng`
- [TryRng](https://docs.rs/trait.TryRng.html)
- Base trait for random number generators and random data sources

## Functions[§](https://docs.rs#functions)

- [fill](https://docs.rs/fn.fill.html)- `thread_rng`
- Fill any type implementing `Fill`
- [make_](https://docs.rs/fn.make_rng.html)- rng - `sys_rng`
- Construct and seed an RNG
- [random](https://docs.rs/fn.random.html)- `thread_rng`
- Generate a random value using the thread-local random number generator.
- [random_](https://docs.rs/fn.random_bool.html)- bool - `thread_rng`
- Return a bool with a probability `p`of being true.
- [random_](https://docs.rs/fn.random_iter.html)- iter - `thread_rng`
- Return an iterator over `random()`
- [random_](https://docs.rs/fn.random_range.html)- range - `thread_rng`
- Generate a random value in the given range using the thread-local random number generator.
- [random_](https://docs.rs/fn.random_ratio.html)- ratio - `thread_rng`
- Return a bool with a probability of `numerator/denominator`of being true.
- [rng](https://docs.rs/fn.rng.html)- `thread_rng`
- Access a fast, pre-initialized generator

# random in rand - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand/^0.8.5/fn.random.html

`pub fn random<T>() -> T`**crate features**only.

`std` and `std_rng`## Expand description

Generates a random value using the thread-local random number generator.

This is simply a shortcut for `thread_rng().gen()`. See [ thread_rng](https://docs.rs/fn.thread_rng.html) for
documentation of the entropy source and

[for documentation of distributions and type-specific generation.](https://docs.rs/distributions/struct.Standard.html)

`Standard`[§](https://docs.rs#provided-implementations)Provided implementations

The following types have provided implementations that generate values with the following ranges and distributions:

- Integers (`i32`,`u32`,`isize`,`usize`, etc.): Uniformly distributed over all values of the type.
- `char`: Uniformly distributed over all Unicode scalar values, i.e. all code points in the range- `0...0x10_FFFF`, except for the range- `0xD800...0xDFFF`(the surrogate code points). This includes unassigned/reserved code points.
- `bool`: Generates- `false`or- `true`, each with probability 0.5.
- Floating point types (`f32`and`f64`): Uniformly distributed in the half-open range`[0, 1)`. See notes below.
- Wrapping integers (`Wrapping<T>`), besides the type identical to their normal integer variants.

Also supported is the generation of the following compound types where all component types are supported:

- Tuples (up to 12 elements): each element is generated sequentially.
- Arrays (up to 32 elements): each element is generated sequentially;
see also `Rng::fill``u32`and smaller types.
- `Option<T>`first generates a- `bool`, and if true generates and returns- `Some(value)`where- `value: T`, otherwise returning- `None`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples)Examples

```
let x = rand::random::<u8>();
println!("{}", x);
let y = rand::random::<f64>();
println!("{}", y);
if rand::random() { // generates a boolean
    println!("Better lucky than good!");
}
```
If you’re calling `random()` in a loop, caching the generator as in the
following example can increase performance.

```
use rand::Rng;
let mut v = vec![1, 2, 3];
for x in v.iter_mut() {
    *x = rand::random()
}
// can be made faster by caching thread_rng
let mut rng = rand::thread_rng();
for x in v.iter_mut() {
    *x = rng.gen();
}
```

`std` and `std_rng`## Expand description

Retrieve the lazily-initialized thread-local random number generator,
seeded by the system. Intended to be used in method chaining style,
e.g. `thread_rng().gen::<i32>()`, or cached locally, e.g.
`let mut rng = thread_rng();`.  Invoked by the `Default` trait, making
`ThreadRng::default()` equivalent.

For more information see [ ThreadRng](https://docs.rs/rngs/struct.ThreadRng.html).

# Rng in rand - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand/^0.8.5/trait.Rng.html

`pub trait Rng: `[RngCore](https://docs.rs/trait.RngCore.html) {
    // Provided methods
    fn [gen](https://docs.rs#method.gen)<T>(&mut self) -> T
       where [Standard](https://docs.rs/distributions/struct.Standard.html): [Distribution](https://docs.rs/distributions/trait.Distribution.html)<T> { ... }
[gen_range](https://docs.rs#method.gen_range)<T, R>(&mut self, range: R) -> T
       where T: [SampleUniform](https://docs.rs/distributions/uniform/trait.SampleUniform.html),
             R: [SampleRange](https://docs.rs/distributions/uniform/trait.SampleRange.html)<T> { ... }
[sample](https://docs.rs#method.sample)<T, D: [Distribution](https://docs.rs/distributions/trait.Distribution.html)<T>>(&mut self, distr: D) -> T { ... }
[sample_iter](https://docs.rs#method.sample_iter)<T, D>(self, distr: D) -> [DistIter](https://docs.rs/distributions/struct.DistIter.html)<D, Self, T> [ⓘ](https://docs.rs)
       where D: [Distribution](https://docs.rs/distributions/trait.Distribution.html)<T>,
             Self: [Sized](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Sized.html) { ... }
[fill](https://docs.rs#method.fill)<T: [Fill](https://docs.rs/trait.Fill.html) + ?[Sized](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Sized.html)>(&mut self, dest: [&mut T](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html)) { ... }
[try_fill](https://docs.rs#method.try_fill)<T: [Fill](https://docs.rs/trait.Fill.html) + ?[Sized](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/marker/trait.Sized.html)>(&mut self, dest: [&mut T](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.reference.html)) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.unit.html), [Error](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html)> { ... }
[gen_bool](https://docs.rs#method.gen_bool)(&mut self, p: [f64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.f64.html)) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html) { ... }
[gen_ratio](https://docs.rs#method.gen_ratio)(&mut self, numerator: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html), denominator: [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html)) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html) { ... }
}## Expand description

An automatically-implemented extension trait on [ RngCore](https://docs.rs/trait.RngCore.html) providing high-level
generic methods for sampling values and other convenience methods.

This is the primary trait to use when generating random values.

[§](https://docs.rs#generic-usage)Generic usage

The basic pattern is `fn foo<R: Rng + ?Sized>(rng: &mut R)`. Some
things are worth noting here:

- Since `Rng: RngCore`and every`RngCore`implements`Rng`, it makes no difference whether we use`R: Rng`or`R: RngCore`.
- The `+ ?Sized`un-bounding allows functions to be called directly on type-erased references; i.e.`foo(r)`where`r: &mut dyn RngCore`. Without this it would be necessary to write`foo(&mut r)`.

An alternative pattern is possible: `fn foo<R: Rng>(rng: R)`. This has some
trade-offs. It allows the argument to be consumed directly without a `&mut`
(which is how `from_rng(thread_rng())` works); also it still works directly
on references (including type-erased references). Unfortunately within the
function `foo` it is not known whether `rng` is a reference type or not,
hence many uses of `rng` require an extra reference, either explicitly
(`distr.sample(&mut rng)`) or implicitly (`rng.gen()`); one may hope the
optimiser can remove redundant references later.

Example:

```
use rand::Rng;
fn foo<R: Rng + ?Sized>(rng: &mut R) -> f32 {
    rng.gen()
}
```
## Provided Methods[§](https://docs.rs#provided-methods)

Return a random value supporting the [ Standard](https://docs.rs/distributions/struct.Standard.html) distribution.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use rand::{thread_rng, Rng};
let mut rng = thread_rng();
let x: u32 = rng.gen();
println!("{}", x);
println!("{:?}", rng.gen::<(f64, bool)>());
```
[§](https://docs.rs#arrays-and-tuples)Arrays and tuples

The `rng.gen()` method is able to generate arrays (up to 32 elements)
and tuples (up to 12 elements), so long as all element types can be
generated.
When using `rustc` ≥ 1.51, enable the `min_const_gen` feature to support
arrays larger than 32 elements.

For arrays of integers, especially for those with small element types
(< 64 bit), it will likely be faster to instead use [ Rng::fill](https://docs.rs/trait.Rng.html#method.fill).

```
use rand::{thread_rng, Rng};
let mut rng = thread_rng();
let tuple: (u8, i32, char) = rng.gen(); // arbitrary tuple support
let arr1: [f32; 32] = rng.gen();        // array construction
let mut arr2 = [0u8; 128];
rng.fill(&mut arr2);                    // array fill
```
Generate a random value in the given range.

This function is optimised for the case that only a single sample is
made from the given range. See also the [ Uniform](https://docs.rs/distributions/struct.Uniform.html) distribution
type which may be faster if sampling from the same range repeatedly.

Only `gen_range(low..high)` and `gen_range(low..=high)` are supported.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics)Panics

Panics if the range is empty.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-1)Example

```
use rand::{thread_rng, Rng};
let mut rng = thread_rng();
// Exclusive range
let n: u32 = rng.gen_range(0..10);
println!("{}", n);
let m: f64 = rng.gen_range(-40.0..1.3e5);
println!("{}", m);
// Inclusive range
let n: u32 = rng.gen_range(0..=10);
println!("{}", n);
```

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rand/rng.rs.html#192-198)#### fn [sample_iter](https://docs.rs#method.sample_iter)<T, D>(self, distr: D) -> [DistIter](https://docs.rs/distributions/struct.DistIter.html)<D, Self, T> [ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/rand/rng.rs.html#192-198)

#### fn [sample_iter](https://docs.rs#method.sample_iter)<T, D>(self, distr: D) -> [DistIter](https://docs.rs/distributions/struct.DistIter.html)<D, Self, T> [ⓘ](https://docs.rs)

Create an iterator that generates values using the given distribution.

Note that this function takes its arguments by value. This works since
`(&mut R): Rng where R: Rng` and
`(&D): Distribution where D: Distribution`,
however borrowing is not automatic hence `rng.sample_iter(...)` may
need to be replaced with `(&mut rng).sample_iter(...)`.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-3)Example

```
use rand::{thread_rng, Rng};
use rand::distributions::{Alphanumeric, Uniform, Standard};
let mut rng = thread_rng();
// Vec of 16 x f32:
let v: Vec<f32> = (&mut rng).sample_iter(Standard).take(16).collect();
// String:
let s: String = (&mut rng).sample_iter(Alphanumeric)
    .take(7)
    .map(char::from)
    .collect();
// Combined values
println!("{:?}", (&mut rng).sample_iter(Standard).take(5)
                             .collect::<Vec<(f64, bool)>>());
// Dice-rolling:
let die_range = Uniform::new_inclusive(1, 6);
let mut roll_die = (&mut rng).sample_iter(die_range);
while roll_die.next().unwrap() != 6 {
    println!("Not a 6; rolling again!");
}
```

Return a bool with a probability of `numerator/denominator` of being
true. I.e. `gen_ratio(2, 3)` has chance of 2 in 3, or about 67%, of
returning true. If `numerator == denominator`, then the returned value
is guaranteed to be `true`. If `numerator == 0`, then the returned
value is guaranteed to be `false`.

See also the [ Bernoulli](https://docs.rs/distributions/struct.Bernoulli.html) distribution, which may be faster if
sampling from the same

`numerator` and `denominator` repeatedly.[§](https://docs.rs#panics-2)Panics

If `denominator == 0` or `numerator > denominator`.

Error type of random number generators

In order to be compatible with `std` and `no_std`, this type has two
possible implementations: with `std` a boxed `Error` trait object is stored,
while with `no_std` we merely store an error code.

# CryptoRng in rand - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand/^0.8.5/trait.CryptoRng.html

`pub trait CryptoRng { }`## Expand description

A marker trait used to indicate that an [ RngCore](https://docs.rs/trait.RngCore.html) or

[implementation is supposed to be cryptographically secure.](https://docs.rs/rand_core/0.6.4/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/rand_core/block/trait.BlockRngCore.html)

`BlockRngCore`*Cryptographically secure generators*, also known as *CSPRNGs*, should
satisfy an additional properties over other generators: given the first
*k* bits of an algorithm’s output
sequence, it should not be possible using polynomial-time algorithms to
predict the next bit with probability significantly greater than 50%.

Some generators may satisfy an additional property, however this is not
required by this trait: if the CSPRNG’s state is revealed, it should not be
computationally-feasible to reconstruct output prior to this. Some other
generators allow backwards-computation and are considered *reversible*.

Note that this trait is provided for guidance only and cannot guarantee suitability for cryptographic applications. In general it should only be implemented for well-reviewed code implementing well-regarded algorithms.

Note also that use of a `CryptoRng` does not protect against other
weaknesses such as seeding from a weak entropy source or leaking state.

# RngCore in rand - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/rand/^0.8.5/trait.RngCore.html

```
pub trait RngCore {
    // Required methods
    fn
```
[next_u32](https://docs.rs#tymethod.next_u32)(&mut self) -> [u32](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u32.html);
[next_u64](https://docs.rs#tymethod.next_u64)(&mut self) -> [u64](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u64.html);
[fill_bytes](https://docs.rs#tymethod.fill_bytes)(&mut self, dest: &mut [[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)]);
[try_fill_bytes](https://docs.rs#tymethod.try_fill_bytes)(&mut self, dest: &mut [[u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html)]) -> [Result](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/result/enum.Result.html)<[()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.unit.html), [Error](https://docs.rs/struct.Error.html)>;
}## Expand description

The core of a random number generator.

This trait encapsulates the low-level functionality common to all
generators, and is the “back end”, to be implemented by generators.
End users should normally use the `Rng` trait from the [ rand](https://docs.rs/rand) crate,
which is automatically implemented for every type implementing

`RngCore`.Three different methods for generating random data are provided since the
optimal implementation of each is dependent on the type of generator. There
is no required relationship between the output of each; e.g. many
implementations of [ fill_bytes](https://docs.rs/trait.RngCore.html#tymethod.fill_bytes) consume a whole number of

`u32` or `u64`
values and drop any remaining unused bytes. The same can happen with the
[and](https://docs.rs/trait.RngCore.html#tymethod.next_u32)

`next_u32`[methods, implementations may discard some random bits for efficiency.](https://docs.rs/trait.RngCore.html#tymethod.next_u64)

`next_u64`The [ try_fill_bytes](https://docs.rs/trait.RngCore.html#tymethod.try_fill_bytes) method is a variant of

[allowing error handling; it is not deemed sufficiently useful to add equivalents for](https://docs.rs/trait.RngCore.html#tymethod.fill_bytes)

`fill_bytes`[or](https://docs.rs/trait.RngCore.html#tymethod.next_u32)

`next_u32`[since the latter methods are almost always used with algorithmic generators (PRNGs), which are normally infallible.](https://docs.rs/trait.RngCore.html#tymethod.next_u64)

`next_u64`Implementers should produce bits uniformly. Pathological RNGs (e.g. always
returning the same value, or never setting certain bits) can break rejection
sampling used by random distributions, and also break other RNGs when
seeding them via [ SeedableRng::from_rng](https://docs.rs/trait.SeedableRng.html#method.from_rng).

Algorithmic generators implementing [ SeedableRng](https://docs.rs/trait.SeedableRng.html) should normally have

*portable, reproducible*output, i.e. fix Endianness when converting values to avoid platform differences, and avoid making any changes which affect output (except by communicating that the release has breaking changes).

Typically an RNG will implement only one of the methods available
in this trait directly, then use the helper functions from the
[ impls](https://docs.rs/rand_core/0.6.4/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/rand_core/impls/index.html) module to implement the other methods.

It is recommended that implementations also implement:

- `Debug`with a custom implementation which- *does not*print any internal state (at least,- `CryptoRng`- `Debug`).
- `Serialize`and- `Deserialize`(from Serde), preferably making Serde support optional at the crate level in PRNG libs.
- `Clone`, if possible.
- *never*implement- `Copy`(accidental copies may cause repeated values).
- *do not*implement- `Default`for pseudorandom generators, but instead implement- `SeedableRng`- `Default`.
- `Eq`and- `PartialEq`could be implemented, but are probably not useful.

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

A simple example, obviously not generating very *random* output:

```
#![allow(dead_code)]
use rand_core::{RngCore, Error, impls};
struct CountingRng(u64);
impl RngCore for CountingRng {
    fn next_u32(&mut self) -> u32 {
        self.next_u64() as u32
    }
    fn next_u64(&mut self) -> u64 {
        self.0 += 1;
        self.0
    }
    fn fill_bytes(&mut self, dest: &mut [u8]) {
        impls::fill_bytes_via_next(self, dest)
    }
    fn try_fill_bytes(&mut self, dest: &mut [u8]) -> Result<(), Error> {
        Ok(self.fill_bytes(dest))
    }
}
```

`RngCore::try_fill_bytes`This method should guarantee that `dest` is entirely filled
with new data, and may panic if this is impossible
(e.g. reading past the end of a file that is being used as the
source of randomness).

Fill `dest` entirely with random data.

This is the only method which allows an RNG to report errors while
generating random data thus making this the primary method implemented
by external (true) RNGs (e.g. `OsRng`) which can fail. It may be used
directly to generate keys and to seed (infallible) PRNGs.

Other than error handling, this method is identical to [ RngCore::fill_bytes](https://docs.rs/trait.RngCore.html#tymethod.fill_bytes);
thus this may be implemented using

`Ok(self.fill_bytes(dest))` or

# SeedableRng in rand - Rust
